claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel is a low-carbon steel.
As-received Q235 steel has a relatively coarse and heterogeneous grain structure.
Controlled annealing refines the grain-boundary structure of Q235 steel.
Corrosion protection of Q235 steel during 700–900 °C salt exposure is governed by an adherent, continuous oxide layer associated with refined grain boundaries.
High-temperature exposure to 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl can produce surface oxide products.
Uniformly distributed grain boundaries act as preferential sites for formation of a continuous, adherent oxide film.
A continuous, adherent oxide film impedes ingress of corrosive species during high-temperature salt exposure.
Impeded ingress of corrosive species mitigates mass change in Q235 steel.
Coarser, irregular grain boundaries in as-received Q235 favor discontinuous oxide formation.
Discontinuous oxide formation promotes scale spallation and accelerated corrosion.
Annealed Q235 steel will form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale than non-annealed Q235 steel under identical high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will have lower mass change and lower corrosion rates than non-annealed Q235 steel.
The proposed grain-boundary passivation mechanism applies primarily under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under ambient, aqueous, or low-salt conditions because different corrosion mechanisms dominate there.
Moisture-induced passivation can be dominant under ambient-temperature conditions.
Salt chemistry and exposure duration can modulate the effectiveness of the proposed grain-boundary passivation mechanism.
